title: The Widow's Gift and the Temple's End
summary: Jesus watches a poor widow give two small coins and says she has given more than all the rich. When his disciples admire the temple's beauty, he predicts that not one stone will be left on another, then describes coming deceivers, wars, persecution, the siege and fall of Jerusalem, and the coming of the Son of Man. He urges them to endure, to keep watch, and to pray.
story: This is Jesus' last public teaching in Luke before the Passover and his arrest. It follows directly from his warning about scribes who devour widows' houses (20:47), and the widow who gives all she has stands as both an example of devotion and a sign of how the system had failed her. From the temple's treasury the conversation moves to the temple itself, and Jesus looks ahead to two events: the destruction of Jerusalem, which would come within a generation, and the coming of the Son of Man at the end of the age. The chapter prepares the disciples to live faithfully in the long period between his departure and his return, the period Luke will describe in Acts.
historical:
Herod the Great's rebuilding of the temple, begun about 20 or 19 BC, made it one of the most impressive buildings in the Roman world. Its platform was enlarged with enormous retaining walls, some of whose stones still stand at the Western Wall in Jerusalem, and the sanctuary was faced with white stone and gold. Wealthy donors gave dedicated gifts that adorned it. Work on the complex continued for decades after Jesus' death.

In AD 66 Judea revolted against Rome. After an initial Roman advance under Cestius Gallus was driven back, the future emperor Vespasian and then his son Titus led the campaign that ended with the siege and capture of Jerusalem in AD 70. The temple was burned and the city largely destroyed, and many of its people were killed or sold as slaves, as Josephus, who witnessed the war, describes. Luke's version of Jesus' warning speaks plainly of Jerusalem surrounded by armies, where Mark speaks of the abomination that causes desolation. A later tradition recorded by the church historian Eusebius says that the Christians of Jerusalem fled the city before the siege to Pella, east of the Jordan.
cultural:
The temple treasury included collection chests in the Court of the Women, where both men and women could go, into which worshipers dropped offerings. The widow's two small copper coins were lepta, the smallest coins in circulation; together they were worth a tiny fraction of a laborer's daily wage. Widows had little means of support unless family cared for them, which makes her gift of all she had to live on remarkable.

Jesus' description of cosmic signs, the sun, moon, and stars shaken and the sea roaring, uses the language of Old Testament prophecy, where such imagery describes God's intervention in history and the fall of powers (Isaiah 13:10, Joel 2:10). Readers debate how literally such language is meant, but its first readers would have recognized a familiar prophetic register. The fig tree, whose leaves appear in late spring, was a common sign that summer was near.
literary: The chapter opens with a brief scene (verses 1 to 4) and then gives the longest block of teaching in Luke's account of Jesus' final days, a discourse about the future often called the Olivet discourse from its setting in Matthew and Mark. Luke's version moves in stages. First come false messiahs, wars, and disasters, which are not yet the end (verses 8 to 11). Before all that, persecution of the disciples (verses 12 to 19). Then the siege and fall of Jerusalem (verses 20 to 24), and after the times of the Gentiles, signs in the heavens and the coming of the Son of Man (verses 25 to 28). A parable of the fig tree and a call to watchfulness close the discourse. The genre combines prophecy and apocalyptic, a style of writing that uses vivid symbols to reveal God's purposes in history and its end.

outline.t: The temple's destruction foretold; signs that are not yet the end
The coming of the Son of Man
The parable of the fig tree

doctrines.note: When the signs begin, Jesus' followers are to stand up and lift their heads, because their redemption is drawing near. The coming of the Son of Man is not only a threat but the promise of rescue.

The fall of Jerusalem is described as days of vengeance and wrath, fulfilling what the prophets had written. Judgment in history anticipates the final judgment, when all will stand before the Son of Man.

Jesus promises his disciples persecution, betrayal by family, and even death, yet says not a hair of their head will perish. The promise is not immunity from suffering but ultimate safety in God's hands, gained through patient endurance.

words.note: Hupomonē, endurance or perseverance, literally remaining under a load. It is not passive waiting but steady faithfulness under pressure. By your patient endurance you will gain your souls: the disciples' lives are secured not by escaping trial but by holding on through it.

Apolutrōsis, redemption, the release of a captive by payment or intervention. Here it names the final deliverance that arrives with the Son of Man. Paul uses the same word for the redemption believers already have in Christ and for the redemption of the body still awaited.

Genea, generation. This generation will not pass away until all these things have happened. Most often in the Gospels the word refers to the people living at that time. Some interpreters give it a wider sense, such as a kind of people or the Jewish people as a whole. How to read it is the chapter's central difficulty, discussed below.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus as a prophet whose word outlasts creation: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.” That is a claim no ordinary prophet would make; in Isaiah 40 it is the word of the Lord that stands forever. He also presents himself as the Son of Man of Daniel 7, who will come in a cloud with power and great glory. Yet he speaks these words days before his own suffering. The one who will be judged by the council and by Pilate is the one before whom all people will finally stand. And his care for the widow, noticed when no one else noticed her, shows the kind of king who is coming.

hard.q: Jesus said this generation would not pass away until all these things happened. Was he mistaken about the timing of his return?
hard.a: This is one of the most discussed sayings in the Gospels, and Christians who share the same confession about Jesus answer it differently. Some take all these things to refer to the events surrounding Jerusalem's fall in AD 70, which did happen within a generation, and read the cosmic imagery as prophetic language for that judgment (the preterist view in its partial form). Others see a double horizon: Jesus speaks of the near event and the final one together, as the prophets often did, with the fall of Jerusalem a foretaste of the end. Still others read generation in a wider sense, as the kind of people who reject him or the Jewish people, who will continue until his return. Luke's own arrangement suggests a gap between the two events, since Jerusalem is trodden down until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled (verse 24). What the text makes clear is that Jesus urged watchfulness, not calculation, and that the fall of Jerusalem he predicted came to pass.

questions: Jesus measured the widow's gift by what she had left, not by what she gave. How would that measure change the way you think about generosity?
The disciples admired stones that would soon be thrown down. What impressive things in your world might look different in the light of Jesus' words?
Jesus warns that hearts can be weighed down by dissipation and the worries of life. Which of those is more likely to dull your attention, and why?
